newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia central bank sells down gold reserves.
newsitem.headline: Australia central bank sells down gold reserves.

text.p: The Reserve Bank of Australia became on Friday the latest in a line of central banks to sell down its gold hoard, saying it saw no reason for a gold-rich country to hold significant official reserves in the metal.
In a statement, the RBA said it had sold 167 tonnes of gold -- more than two-thirds of its holdings -- over the past six months, but no further sales were planned.
At current prices, the gold was worth some US$1.8 billion.

News of the sale came with gold bullion trading at near four-year lows on international bullion markets -- caused in part by market fears that gold was losing its shine for central bankers out to protect their currencies.
Various central banks including those of Canada and Belgium have sold off gold in recent years.
Market nervousness has been increased by German and Swiss plans to revalue official gold reserves, in Switzerland's case to help pay compensation to Holocaust victims.

But bullion was marked up slightly higher at the London afternoon fix -- at US$332.55 against a morning fix of US$332.30 -- after rumours of the Australian gold sales. Dealers said the market had been trading short and welcomed the extra supply.
The Australian central bank said its case was a special one: in brief, the world's third-largest producer would never run out of gold and did not need vast reserves.

"The Australian sales program followed a review by the Bank of the costs and benefits of holding a significant part of international reserves in the form of gold," the RBA said in a statement announcing the sales.
It said its board had concluded that although some gold was worth holding as a contingency, it no longer needed to have 20 percent of its overall international reserves in the metal.

"The principal reason for this conclusion was that a country in Australia's position, with large gold reserves in the ground and high annual production, derives negligible diversification benefits from holding a significant proportion of its international reserves in the form of gold," the RBA said.
Australian Treasurer Peter Costello said the RBA had sought his approval to reinvest the proceeds of the sale in foreign currency assets, rather than paying the government a windfall budget dividend.

"While such a dividend would have made a major boost to the Commonwealth (Australian national) budget, it would have been fiscally and prudentially irresponsible to have followed that course of action," Costello said in a statement.
"Such a dividend would have only been a one-off assistance to the budget in the year it was paid.

"Payment of such a dividend would have eroded the official reserve position of the RBA, and weakened its balance sheet which underpins Australia's financial system, and its standing in world markets."
Compared with worldwide official central bank reserves estimated at 35,000 tonnes, the Australian sales were not significant in volume.

But they still represented more than half of the 300-odd tonnes produced annually in Australia and could yet take on a symbolic importance for markets already unsettled by gold sales from central banks in Belgium, Canada, Austria, the Netherlands, Portugal and South Africa.
"This (sale) should be bullish because the market is so short but, equally, the market might say 'that is Australia, who is next'," said one European dealer.

"The market hasn't done much. I think the market's a little bit short at the moment and that's why reaction has been muted," added an Australian dealer after announcement at midnight Australian time (1400 GMT).

The RBA's move looked unlikely to find favour among domestic miners, many of whom are already struggling to turn a profit given the weak gold price and a strong local dollar. Miners could well accuse the bank of undercutting their market.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
